Office Hours

By eight in the morning, two queues had already formed outside the district administration. One was waiting for certificates confirming payments to reservists' families; the other was trying to find out exactly who the new call-up would affect. The secretary brought a second chair into the corridor, placed an inkwell on the windowsill and began writing down names on the back of an old poster. The direct telephone line to the capital had been silent all morning.

Three documents lay on the district chief's desk which, in the past, would not even have reached discussion without presidential permission. An emergency fund had to be opened after a road collapsed, a doctor's appointment to a mountain settlement confirmed, and fuel released to a reserve battalion. The requests had been sent yesterday. No reply had arrived.

At noon, new forms arrived from the capital. Every one still bore the printed name of Pyotr Ivanov. The district chief took the first sheet, stared for a long time at the empty signature line, then wrote his own surname and added: 'On the instructions of the presidential administration.' He had received no such instructions. An hour later, seven more documents had been processed in the same way.

No one called it disobedience. People needed their money, the road needed repairing, and fuel had to be issued. The state kept working because its officials were gradually learning to make decisions that had once existed only after one man's signature.

By evening, the telephone from the capital still had not rung. The queues were booked in again for tomorrow.
The work continued in the name of a man who no longer directed it.
A Place at the Table

Twelve cups were set out for the morning meeting, as usual. Ministers and department heads took eleven places. The twelfth cup remained before the chairman's empty seat.

Ivanov's assistant opened a folder and began reading the agenda. The first item required the president's signature. So did the second. Attached to the third was a note from the War Ministry requesting confirmation of an order issued several days earlier. No one in the room knew whether Ivanov would see any of these papers.

In the past, a meeting like this would have stopped. A decision taken without the president was considered provisional, and a document without his signature was returned to its sender. Today, Hedersett asked the assistant to continue. One minister objected. Another pointed out that the port could not wait for the chairman's recovery. Within minutes, those present were allocating expenditure, appointing officials and approving orders Ivanov had never seen.

No one uttered the word 'successor'. There was no need.

By the end of the meeting, the papers were no longer in front of the empty chair. They lay before Hedersett. The president's assistant noticed first. He said nothing and simply continued taking the minutes.

After the meeting, an attendant began collecting the cups. When she reached Ivanov's place, she paused for a moment. The cup was untouched. Tomorrow's list still called for twelve.

But for the first time in decades, eleven people had governed Stelander for an entire day.
The country was learning to live without the man who was still its president.
Call in Ainholm's Forces
The Ainholm Mandate's forces will enter the northern war on our side. The colony's participation will end with the northern campaign.
District Council Authority
The districts supply their own units and retain civilian administration. Proximity to local depots eases supply, but the joint headquarters must coordinate its orders with several councils.
Emergency Headquarters Powers

Kefreyt's attack forced the councils to entrust the coordination of defence to headquarters. Commanders organise unit rotations and a common operational plan. These powers last only until the war with Kefreyt ends; Shabrat's victory or defeat does not revoke them.
Paid Supplies for the Districts

Shabrat's government has paid for weapons and work at local workshops. For 42 days, military factory output increases by 20% and organisation recovery by 10%. The programme ends when the war against Kefreyt is over or independence is lost.
Guarantees to the District Councils

The pre-war agreement survived the split. Shabrat promised to preserve the councils' autonomy and gained the ability to finance their supplies if Kefreyt attacks. Once civilian government returns, a decision must be made on whether that promise will become a permanent charter.
Charter of District Cooperation

Stelander has recognised the republics' independence. Joint orders and agreements between workshops accelerate civilian industrial construction on both sides. The charter does not create a military alliance or draw its signatories into one another's wars.
Central Government Powers

The government has refused to formalise its commitments to the district councils. Unified state procurement increases military factory output by 10% and reduces administrative expenditure by 5%. The republics are no longer promised supplies or joint programmes.
Distrust of Stelander

Shabrat's government has retreated from its pre-war guarantees. The councils are strengthening the defence of their own territories and preparing to rely on themselves. Refusing the charter does not, in itself, start another war.
Fund Supplies for the Republics

For 300 treasury units, we will purchase supplies from private vendors for the republics: 1200 rifles and 30 support equipment will reach their stockpiles. District workshops and unit recovery will receive support for 42 days. Our own weapons stockpile is not spent. Another shipment may be funded after 42 days if the republics' war with Kefreyt is still ongoing.
Both sides are independent and honour the agreement; the republics are at war with Kefreyt, have not capitulated and have completed their previous supply programme

Negotiate a District Charter
Civilian government has been restored. We can now return to the pre-war guarantees and settle relations with the independent republics. Their separate war with Kefreyt does not prevent negotiations.
Shabrat has defeated the Party; both sides are independent, have not capitulated, maintain the pre-war guarantees and are not already in negotiations
Signatures on the Charter

The district council representatives brought a copy of the agreement signed before the split. The paper has yellowed along its folds; beside Shabrat's signature are those of the people who kept local government running throughout it all.

The councils now propose to confirm the republics' independence and open joint procurement for civilian workshops. The document does not include a military alliance. The central chancellery proposes concentrating orders at our own military factories and reducing consultation with districts which no longer answer to the capital. Refusing the charter will end assistance to the councils.

The representatives await an answer. The war changed the map, but the signatures remain the same.
Confirm the guarantees and sign the charter.
Leave these matters to the central chancellery.
Circumstances have changed.
A Letter from the District Councils

The letter arrived with a lorry driver. The councils confirmed the pre-war agreement: the republics would govern their own districts independently, while Shabrat would maintain his promised guarantees.\n\nA list of workshops and depots was attached on the reverse. If Kefreyt attacks, paid arms shipments can be organised through them. At the bottom, a different hand had added: 'We will still need the agreement after the war.'

The district councils' letter contains no request for a governor to be appointed. The republics announced the formation of their own administration and proposed avoiding clashes along the border.\n\nThe military demands a common defence plan; local representatives want to retain control of supplies and personnel. If Kefreyt attacks, headquarters will receive emergency powers, but the councils have no intention of dissolving themselves. Victory in the capital will not settle their future.
Acknowledged.

At least one of the three campaigns remains unused, and its electoral stage has begun. Shabrat's second campaign requires an administration in Monaya or Niansas; the third requires both. Each required administration must have operated continuously for 21 days.

Military Committee Funds

The military proposes using funds raised by supporters to equip an assault formation. The committee will receive the money immediately, but civilian delegates will see this as preparation for a seizure of power. Construction of our own workshops will have to wait.
